profile.name: Mina S.
profile.tagline: Incoming electrical engineering student in Canada with a growing interest in cybersecurity, digital citizenship, and responsible technology.
profile.definition: To me, digital citizenship means combining technical skill with responsibility. It includes checking information before sharing it, protecting privacy, using technology ethically, and contributing to online spaces in ways that make them safer and more respectful.
profile.mission: My mission is to grow as an engineer and digital citizen at the same time. I want the way I learn, build, and communicate online to reflect curiosity, care, and cybersecurity awareness.
profile.aboutTitle: Incoming first-year electrical engineering student in Canada
aboutText: I am Mina Soliman, an incoming first-year electrical engineering student studying in Canada. I am interested in how engineering can solve practical problems while still protecting the people who rely on those systems.

Cybersecurity is one of the areas that excites me most because it connects technical design with trust, privacy, and accountability. That interest naturally connects to digital citizenship, which gives me a framework for how I want to participate online.
This website brings those interests together. It tracks how I learn, reflect, and contribute so my growth in digital citizenship stays visible, measurable, and grounded in real habits.

home.projectSummary: This project turns digital citizenship into something visible and accountable. As I prepare to begin electrical engineering in Canada, I use the site to connect my interest in cybersecurity with reflection, measurable habits, and positive online participation.

personalGoals: Keep source verification consistent enough that I can explain why I trust what I share.
Treat privacy settings as a repeated maintenance task instead of a one-time setup step.
Use AI as a support tool only when I can still account for accuracy, authorship, and impact.
Contribute at least one useful resource, walkthrough, or peer-support action every week.
codeOfConduct: Verify before sharing, especially when content is emotionally charged or urgent.
Protect private information and ask for consent before reposting or forwarding someone else's content.
Credit ideas, code, and creative work clearly.
Use disagreement to clarify, not to embarrass or escalate.
Pause when a tool saves time but weakens responsibility.
principles: I will verify information before sharing it.
I will use technology in ways that help rather than harm.
I will protect my privacy and respect other people's privacy.
I will contribute positively to online communities.
I will be transparent about the role of AI and automation in my work.
I will practice consent in digital spaces, not just compliance.
I will reflect on how my digital habits affect myself and others.

reflections.title: Reviewing my digital footprint before the next school year
content: As I look ahead to starting electrical engineering in Canada, I wanted to review what I am publicly attaching to my name online. That meant checking bios, old posts, shared profiles, and the tone of the spaces where I participate most.

The goal was not to erase personality, but to make sure my digital footprint reflects the kind of learner and community member I want to be: curious, responsible, and increasingly aware of cybersecurity and digital citizenship.

reflections.title: Cross-checking AI summaries before I trust them
content: AI summaries are useful for orientation, but they often compress uncertainty out of a topic. This week I started checking every summary against at least one primary source before I reuse any claim.
That extra step slowed me down slightly, but it improved my confidence and made my notes more accurate. Convenience is only ethical when it still leaves room for responsibility.

reflections.title: Reducing passive screen time after 9 PM
content: I noticed that tired scrolling made me less thoughtful about what I liked, shared, and clicked. I replaced late-night scrolling with a short shutdown checklist and one intentional article or video.
The change helped me separate rest from distraction and made my online time feel more chosen than automatic.

reflections.title: Revisiting privacy defaults on every new app
content: I used to treat privacy setup as a one-time task, but every new app quietly adds fresh decisions. I now check visibility, permissions, contact sync, and notification settings before I start using a service regularly.
That routine turns privacy from a vague value into a repeatable behavior.

reflections.title: Writing clearer and kinder replies in group chats
content: Short messages travel fast, and tone gets flattened easily. I started pausing before sending corrections or reminders, especially in group chats where public friction can grow quickly.
Being concise does not require being sharp. Clear and respectful replies reduce noise and help people stay engaged.

reflections.title: When productivity tools become distractions
content: I spent too much time tuning tools that were supposed to save time. The problem was not the apps themselves, but the way I kept optimizing instead of doing the work.
I now ask whether a tool improves clarity, safety, or output quality. If it mainly adds novelty, I treat it as optional.

reflections.title: Helping classmates cite sources in a shared document
content: A shared study document was growing quickly, but sources were inconsistent. I added a simple citation pattern and a note explaining why link quality matters when notes get reused.
The fix was small, but it made the document more trustworthy and easier for everyone to build on.

reflections.title: Slowing down before repeating fast-moving stories
content: A story moved quickly through class chats this week, and my first instinct was to repeat it before I had checked the source. I stopped, looked for the original report, and realized the summary being shared had left out important context.
That moment reminded me that media literacy is often about slowing down when everyone else is speeding up. Accuracy is part of respect.

reflections.title: Treating password hygiene like regular maintenance
content: I used to think about passwords mostly when a site forced me to update one. This month I started treating password checks as maintenance: review reused passwords, confirm multi-factor authentication, and update recovery methods.
Cybersecurity feels more manageable when I break it into repeated habits instead of waiting for a problem to force a reaction.

reflections.title: Resetting notification habits after winter break
content: After winter break I noticed I was reaching for my phone more often than I wanted, mostly because notifications kept interrupting study time. I reviewed which apps actually deserve immediate attention and turned most of the rest into scheduled check-ins.
The change felt small, but it gave me more control over attention and made my online time feel intentional again.

reflections.title: Making a shared troubleshooting guide instead of repeating the same fixes
content: A few of us kept running into the same digital tool issues, and I realized I was typing the same answers over and over. I turned those answers into a short shared guide with steps, screenshots, and a note on safe account setup.
Helping once is useful, but documenting a solution can help more people with less friction.

reflections.title: Using AI for study support without outsourcing my thinking
content: I experimented with using AI to organize study questions and explain unfamiliar terms, but I kept noticing how easy it was to let the tool become the voice of the work. That is useful for speed, but risky for learning.
I set a simple rule for myself: AI can help me start, compare, or check, but it should not replace the part where I explain the idea in my own words.

reflections.title: Reviewing location permissions before convenience becomes the default
content: I realized several apps had access to my location even though they did not need it all the time. It happened gradually because tapping allow was easier than thinking through the tradeoff in the moment.
This reflection pushed me to switch more apps to while-using or never. Privacy is often decided in the tiny moments when convenience asks for less thought.

reflections.title: Checking captions and claims before reposting
content: I noticed how easy it is to repost something because it sounds right or matches the mood of the moment. This week I made myself read beyond the caption before sharing anything that sounded factual or urgent.
That small pause changed how I think about participation online. Sharing is not neutral when other people may trust the signal I send.

reflections.title: Why I started tracking digital citizenship deliberately
content: I wanted a way to think more seriously about the kind of person I am online, not just the things I post. Digital citizenship felt like the right starting point because it connects behavior, safety, community, and reflection.
Beginning this log made the topic feel practical. Instead of treating good online behavior as a vague ideal, I could start recording choices, patterns, and improvements over time.
